title: Remote Work Is Making Americans Lonelier and More Depressed — and the Effect Is Worst for Those Who Live Alone
excerpt: A sweeping study of 588,000 workers finds that the shift to working from home accounts for a third of the rise in national mental distress since 2011. For Indian-origin tech workers thousands of miles from family, the findings hit close to home.
body:
The convenience of working from home may be exacting a steeper psychological toll than most people realise. A landmark study of more than 588,000 American workers, published in the journal *Science*, has found that remote work significantly increases social isolation, loneliness and mental distress — and the effects are especially severe for people who live alone.

The research, led by economists at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, the University of Virginia and Harvard University, drew on five nationally representative surveys conducted between 2011 and 2024, excluding the peak pandemic years of 2020 and 2021 to isolate the effects of remote work itself from the chaos of lockdowns.

Their central finding is stark. Workers in "remotable" jobs — roles that could shift to home-based work, such as software engineering and marketing — now spend roughly an extra hour alone on each workday compared to workers in in-person roles like nursing or mechanical engineering. They do not compensate for that lost social contact after hours.

"We even see a decrease in spending time with friends after the workday relative to people in non-remotable occupations," said lead author Natalia Emanuel, an economist at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

## The Loneliness Multiplier

The data reveals something even more troubling. Nearly nine in ten workers in remotable jobs spend their entire workday completely alone. For those who live alone — a rapidly growing demographic — the isolation compounds dramatically. Their pandemic-prompted increase in days spent alone was ten times that experienced by workers living with other people.

Some workers described going entire days without a single face-to-face interaction of any kind — "not even like a wave to a barista, not somebody also checking for ripeness of the avocados at the grocery store," Emanuel told NPR.

The mental health consequences are measurable. Compared to workers in non-remotable jobs, those who could work from home reported higher rates of psychological distress, were more likely to visit a mental health professional, and filled more prescriptions for antidepressants and anti-anxiety medications. The researchers estimate that the rise of remote work accounts for roughly a third of the increase in mental distress across the United States during the study period.

## A Debate, Not a Verdict

The findings have sparked heated debate among researchers. Stanford economist Nick Bloom, who has conducted randomised trials on remote work, argues that the picture is more nuanced. In his studies, workers who were allowed to work remotely reported improved mental health, not worse — benefiting from reduced commuting stress, greater control over their time and more time with family.

"The simple story is when people can work from home, they can reduce commuting stress, control their time better and have more time with friends and family," Bloom said.

The key distinction may be between fully remote and hybrid work. A separate study using 2024 Household Pulse Survey data found that working remotely three or more days per week was associated with significantly higher loneliness, while working remotely just one to two days per week carried no elevated risk.

More than half of remote employees in the United States now work hybrid schedules, spending an average of 2.3 days per week in the office, according to Gallup. That middle ground may offer the flexibility workers want without the isolation costs.

## The Diaspora Dimension

For Indian-origin professionals in the United States, the findings carry particular weight. South Asian immigrants make up a disproportionate share of the technology workforce — precisely the remotable, knowledge-economy roles the study identifies as most affected. Many are first-generation immigrants who left extended family networks in India and depend on workplace relationships for social connection in a new country.

The shift to remote and hybrid work during the pandemic meant that a critical lifeline — daily interactions with colleagues, lunch conversations, after-work socialising — was suddenly severed. For H-1B visa holders who are geographically tied to their employer and may not have established deep local friend networks, the effects can be particularly acute.

Former US Surgeon General Vivek Murthy, himself an Indian-American, declared an epidemic of loneliness in 2023, warning that social isolation raises the risk of depression, anxiety and even premature death at rates comparable to smoking 15 cigarettes a day. The new study confirms that the modern American workplace — reshaped by the pandemic — is one of the key sites where that epidemic is playing out.

## What Experts Recommend

The study's authors and independent experts broadly agree on one point: the answer is not forcing everyone back to the office five days a week. Bloom's research suggests the best approach is giving workers the choice of where to work, since different people have different needs for social interaction.

For remote workers who recognise the toll of isolation, experts recommend proactive steps: scheduling in-person meetups with colleagues, joining community groups or co-working spaces, maintaining a regular exercise routine that gets you out of the house, and deliberately protecting time for social activities rather than letting the workday expand to fill the space.

The study is a reminder that the most valued perk of the modern knowledge economy — the freedom to work from anywhere — may carry hidden costs that only become visible after the novelty fades and the silence settles in.

*Sources: Science (AAAS), Smithsonian Magazine, NPR, USA Today, Gallup*
